Roughly 1 in 3 adults in Pakistan now lives with diabetes — the highest rate anywhere in the world, ahead of the Gulf states and the Pacific islands.

One map, and a story about diet, genetics, and speed — a thread 🧵🗺️

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)
1/ The map shows age-standardized diabetes prevalence among adults 20–79. Pakistan's dark red sits at roughly 31%. Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and the Marshall Islands aren't far behind, all above 20%.

2/ Part of the explanation is genetic. South Asians tend to store more visceral fat and develop insulin resistance at a lower body weight than Europeans — researchers call it the "thin-fat" phenotype. The same BMI carries more risk.

3/ The bigger driver is speed. Pakistan's diet shifted fast toward refined carbs, sugary tea, and fried food, while urbanization cut the physical labor that once burned off those calories. Bodies didn't get generations to adjust.

4/ The Gulf states tell a related but different story: oil wealth compressed decades of dietary and lifestyle change into a few decades, air conditioning and cars replaced walking, and much of the physical labor shifted onto migrant workers.

5/ The Pacific islands add a third thread. Imported processed food displaced traditional diets after WWII, and some researchers point to a "thrifty gene" once useful for surviving famine that now backfires amid food abundance.

6/ Screening and treatment lag behind the disease everywhere on this map's dark end — diabetes is often caught only after complications appear, which is a large part of why it keeps climbing fastest in exactly these countries.
